questions.stem: Given that \(\sin A=t\) and \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\), then \(\cos A\) is:
questions.hint: In the range \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\) (second quadrant), cosine is negative.

steps.explain: Use the Pythagorean identity to express \(\cos A\) in terms of \(\sin A=t\), taking the square root of both sides.
Since \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\) places \(A\) in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative, choose the negative root.

steps.work:

cos θ < 0 ⇒ x-coordinate negative

steps.explain: Apply the co-function identities for each term.

questions.hint: Use \(\sin(90°-x°)=\cos(x°)\), then factorise the numerator (difference of squares, since \(\cos^2x-1=-(1-\cos^2x)=-\sin^2x\), or factor directly as \((\cos x-1)(\cos x+1)\)).

steps.explain: Use the co-function identity \(\sin(90°-x°)=\cos(x°)\) to rewrite the denominator.
Factorise the numerator as a difference of squares.
Cancel the common factor \((\cos x°-1)\).

questions.stem: Solve the equation \(2\cos x°=\cot x°\) for \(0\le x\le360\).
questions.hint: Write \(\cot x°=\dfrac{\cos x°}{\sin x°}\), then factorise the resulting equation — you should get two separate cases to solve.

steps.explain: Rewrite \(\cot x°\) in terms of sine and cosine, then rearrange to have zero on one side.
steps.work: \(2\cos x° = \dfrac{\cos x°}{\sin x°} \Rightarrow 2\cos x°\sin x° - \cos x° = 0\)

steps.explain: Factorise out \(\cos x°\).
Solve each factor separately: \(\cos x°=0\) gives \(x=90,270\); \(\sin x°=\tfrac12\) gives \(x=30,150\).
Combine all four solutions.

questions.stem: On the same set of axes, sketch the graphs of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\), for \(-180°\le x\le180°\), then state the number of solutions to \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) in this domain.

parts.stem: (i) On the same set of axes, sketch the graphs of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\), for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).

steps.explain: \(y=3\sin2x\) has amplitude 3 and period \(180°\) (since the angle is doubled, the period is \(360°/2\)).
steps.work: \(y=3\sin2x\): amplitude 3, period 180°, passing through the origin.

steps.explain: \(y=\cos^2x\) ranges from 0 to 1 only (since it's a square), oscillating with period \(180°\) as well (since \(\cos^2x=\tfrac12(1+\cos2x)\)).
steps.work: \(y=\cos^2x\): range \([0,1]\), period 180°, equal to 1 at \(x=0,\pm180°\) and 0 at \(x=\pm90°\).

steps.explain: Sketch both curves on the same axes over \([-180°,180°]\) — the sine curve swings from \(-3\) to \(3\) while the squared-cosine curve stays flat between 0 and 1.
steps.work: Both curves plotted on \([-180°,180°]\); note where they cross — this is used in part (ii).

parts.stem: (ii) Hence, or otherwise, state the number of solutions to the equation \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).
parts.hint: Solving \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) is the same as finding where the two graphs from part (i) intersect — or factorise algebraically: write \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and take out the common factor \(\cos x\).

steps.explain: Solving \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) is equivalent to finding where the two graphs from part (i) intersect.
steps.work: Count the crossing points of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\) on \([-180°,180°]\).

steps.explain: Algebraically: substitute \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and factorise out \(\cos x\).

\(\cos x=0\) gives 2 solutions in the domain; \(6\sin x=\cos x \Rightarrow \tan x=\tfrac16\) gives another 2 solutions (one from \(\arctan\tfrac16\approx9.5°\), one from adding \(180°\) then wrapping back into range at \(\approx-170.5°\)).
Combine all solutions found.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) there are \(4\) solutions to \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).
